overview: Section A is the base of the whole CIA program. It covers why internal auditing exists, where its authority comes from, what the charter must say, the two kinds of service (assurance, an evidence-based conclusion others can rely on, and advisory, which is advice), what threatens independence, and where internal audit sits in the Three Lines Model. Watch two words throughout: 'must' marks a requirement of the Standards, while 'should' or 'may' marks a consideration, a preferred or optional practice that no answer can call mandatory. It carries the most weight in Part 1, and Parts 2 and 3 build on its rules.
analogy: Think of a building inspector hired by a city council, not by the builders. The council's written order says what the inspector may enter and inspect (the mandate, kept in the charter). The inspector tests the work against the building code and reports what was found (assurance), and may answer a builder's questions about a planned design (advice), but never pours the concrete or signs the builder's plans. If builders could set the inspector's budget, lock doors or choose what gets inspected, nobody could trust the reports. That is why the inspector answers to the council.

topics.overview: Domain I of the Global Internal Audit Standards states in a few lines why internal auditing exists and when it works best. This topic covers what internal audit gives the organization, what it improves, the three conditions for effectiveness, and how the Standards themselves are built.
can_do: Describe what internal auditing provides, to whom, and to what end
List the five things internal auditing enhances in an organization
Explain the three conditions under which internal auditing works best
Tell internal audit's purpose apart from management's job of managing risk and running controls

subtopics.name: The Purpose Statement
subtopics.definition: The Purpose of Internal Auditing is Domain I's short statement of why the profession exists: to make an organization better at creating, protecting and sustaining value.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Every other rule in the Standards serves this purpose. Knowing whom internal audit serves, and with what, rules out answers that turn the internal auditor into a manager or a fraud detective.
how_it_works: Internal auditing gives the board and management four things: assurance, advice, insight and foresight. The work is independent, risk-based and objective.

The statement lists five gains: achieving objectives; stronger governance, risk management and control processes; better decisions and oversight; reputation and credibility; and serving the public interest.
The Standards have five domains, 15 principles and 52 standards. Each standard has requirements ('must') and considerations for implementation ('should' or 'may').
A 'must' is mandatory; a 'should' (preferred practice) or a 'may' (optional) is not a requirement.
subtopics.example: Abena is a new internal auditor at a Ghanaian bus company. At a depot briefing, a supervisor introduces Abena as the person sent to catch fraud and repair faulty procedures. Abena corrects this politely: the team offers the board and management an independent view of how well risks are handled, plus advice, and repairs stay with the depot's managers.

review: Compare the charter's purpose section with Domain I of the Standards
Evaluate whether stakeholder feedback shows internal audit's work was useful
evidence: Charter section that states the Purpose of Internal Auditing
Survey or interview feedback from board members and senior managers
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the chief audit executive to explain the purpose to the board and senior management when the charter is discussed.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the charter that states the purpose

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditing strengthens the organization by giving the board and management independent, risk-based, objective assurance, advice, insight and foresight. Managing risk, running controls and deciding are management's work.

exam_traps.trap: The purpose of internal auditing is to manage the organization's risks and catch fraud.
exam_traps.why: Those are management's jobs. Internal audit assesses and advises on how well they are done. Fraud risk is part of that work.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit works for management only.
exam_traps.why: The statement names the board and management together, and the function is accountable directly to the board.

key_terms.definition: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
A statement, resting on an objective assessment against criteria, that raises confidence in a process.
The person or team that provides internal audit services; 'the function' for short.

subtopics.name: Conditions for Effective Internal Auditing
subtopics.definition: Conditions for effectiveness are the three things Domain I ties to internal auditing at its best: competent professionals following the Standards, independent positioning, and freedom from undue influence.
subtopics.why_it_matters: These conditions explain most governance rules that follow. A function that lacks skill, reports to the wrong level, or can be leaned on produces reports nobody can rely on.
how_it_works: First, the work is done by competent professionals who conform with the Global Internal Audit Standards.
Second, the internal audit function is positioned independently and answers directly to the board.
Third, nobody can pressure internal auditors into a view, and they commit to judging objectively.
Fundamentals of the Standards: anyone doing internal audit work is bound, whether in-house staff, auditors supplied by an outside firm, or both.
The chief audit executive (CAE) answers for the function's conformance; every internal auditor, for the standards relevant to their own work.
Conformance is expected. When a requirement truly cannot be met, the CAE must document and communicate the circumstance, the alternative action, its impact and the reason.
subtopics.example: A family-owned Japanese logistics group set up internal audit under the finance director and told the team to skip the Standards. Later, a fuel purchasing report was rewritten before the owners saw it. Aiko, hired to rebuild it, ties the failure to the missing conditions and proposes skilled staff, a direct line to the board, and protection from pressure.

review: Compare the function's actual reporting line with the charter and board minutes
Inspect training and certification records against the skills the plan needs
evidence: Quality assessment results on conformance with the Standards
Board minutes showing direct sessions with the chief audit executive
audit_focus.recommend: Report gaps in skills, positioning or freedom from pressure to the board, with safeguards the chief audit executive proposes.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides how the function is positioned and supported

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal auditing is most effective when three things hold: competent people conforming with the Standards, an independently positioned function accountable to the board, and internal auditors free from undue influence. Must: the CAE documents and communicates any requirement that cannot be met.

exam_traps.trap: Independent positioning and conformance are good practice that a small or busy function can drop.
exam_traps.why: Domain I names them as conditions for effectiveness, and conformance is expected whatever the function's size. An unmet requirement must be documented and communicated, not ignored.

exam_traps.trap: Independence and objectivity are the same condition.
exam_traps.why: The second condition is about where the function sits (independence). The third is about each auditor's unbiased mindset (objectivity).

key_terms.definition: Meeting the requirements of the Global Internal Audit Standards.
Pressure or interest that pushes a judgment away from the evidence.
The function answers to the board itself, not to the managers it reviews.

topics.topic_name: The mandate and who sets it
topics.overview: The mandate is what internal audit is allowed and expected to do. This topic covers what the mandate contains, where it comes from, how the chief audit executive helps set and refresh it, and what the board and senior management each do. Their duties are called essential conditions: things internal audit needs from them, not rules placed on them. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Explain what a mandate contains and where it comes from
Explain what the chief audit executive supplies so that the mandate can be set, and when it is revisited
Tell the board's part from senior management's part in setting and supporting the mandate
Explain what the chief audit executive does when the board or senior management will not provide an essential condition

subtopics.name: The Internal Audit Mandate
subtopics.definition: The internal audit mandate is the function's authority, role and responsibilities, given by the board, by laws and regulations, or by both.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The mandate is the source of the function's power to audit. Without it, a manager could refuse access or argue that an area is off limits.
how_it_works: Authority comes from the direct reporting line to the board. It brings unrestricted access to the board and to records, people and property.
The role is mainly to deliver internal audit services. Other roles, such as compliance, may be added to the chief audit executive's duties and then need safeguards.
Responsibilities are what the function answers for: performing services, communicating, following laws and policies, and conforming with the Standards.
Scope says how much of the organization is covered and which services are offered, such as assurance alone, or both assurance and advice.
The mandate comes from the board, from law or regulation (common in the public sector), or both, and is recorded in the charter (Standard 6.1 Internal Audit Mandate).
subtopics.example: Thandiwe, a new internal auditor at a South African insurer, is refused claims files by a manager who says the internal audit function has no right to customer data. The board-approved charter says otherwise: the mandate gives unrestricted access to the records the work needs. Thandiwe shows the manager the clause and, when access is still refused, reports the restriction to the engagement supervisor.

review: Trace the function's authority, role and responsibilities to the approved charter
Compare the charter's scope with any mandate set by law or regulation
evidence: Minutes of the board meeting that adopted the mandate
Text of any statute or regulation prescribing internal audit's duties
audit_focus.recommend: Request that senior management and the board resolve any gap between the charter's scope and what the law prescribes.
audit_focus.decides: The board, or lawmakers where the mandate is legal

subtopics.isaca_rule: The mandate is authority, role and responsibilities. It comes from the board, from law, or both, and it lives in the charter. Must: the chief audit executive (CAE) supplies the information and documents the mandate, but does not grant it.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE sets the mandate, because the CAE writes the charter.
exam_traps.why: Drafting is not granting. The board establishes and approves the mandate, unless law or regulation prescribes it.

exam_traps.trap: A mandate must always come from the board.
exam_traps.why: It may be prescribed wholly or partly by laws or regulations, as often happens in the public sector. Then the charter must include those legal requirements.

key_terms.definition: The power to do the work, created by the direct line to the board.
Freedom to reach the data, records, people and property the work needs.
One piece of internal audit work with its own objectives and scope.

subtopics.name: The Chief Audit Executive's Part in Setting the Mandate
subtopics.definition: The chief audit executive's part in the mandate is to supply the information the board and senior management need, record the result in the charter, and keep it current.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A board can only grant a sensible mandate if it understands what the internal audit function can do and what other assurance providers already cover. The chief audit executive (CAE) is the person who knows.
how_it_works: The CAE must give the board and senior management the information needed to establish the mandate, such as what the Standards and the law expect.
Before scope is set, they must work out with the other assurance providers, inside and outside the organization, who covers what.
They must write the mandate into the charter, or reference it there (Standard 6.1 Internal Audit Mandate).
Periodically, they must assess whether changed circumstances call for a fresh discussion of the mandate with the board and senior management.
Typical triggers are changed Standards, an acquisition or reorganization, new board members or senior managers, new strategy or risks, and new laws.
A formal check at least once a year is a should, not a must.
subtopics.example: Mariana becomes CAE of a Brazilian retailer just after it buys an online payments company. Mariana briefs the board and senior management on what the Standards expect, maps what compliance and the external auditor already cover, and proposes adding the payments business to the scope. After the discussion, Mariana updates the draft charter and submits it to the board.

review: Trace each charter change to a documented discussion with the board
Compare the date of the last mandate review with major organizational changes
evidence: Dated record of the yearly check on whether the mandate still fits
Briefing papers on leading practices and on who else gives assurance
audit_focus.recommend: Put the mandate on the board's agenda after any acquisition, restructuring or change of leadership.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides, after hearing senior management's input

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: the CAE informs, coordinates, documents and periodically reassesses the mandate. Should: make a formal check at least once a year. The board decides whether the mandate changes.

exam_traps.trap: Once the board approves the charter, the mandate is settled and need not be discussed again.
exam_traps.why: The CAE must periodically assess whether circumstances justify a new discussion. The considerations suggest a formal look at least once a year.

key_terms.definition: Any internal or external party that gives assurance, such as compliance, risk management or the external auditor.
A practice the Standards' considerations describe as preferred. It is advice, not a requirement.
The periodic check that authority, role and responsibilities still fit the function's strategy and objectives.

subtopics.name: What the Board and Senior Management Each Do
subtopics.definition: Board and senior management roles in the mandate are split: the board discusses and approves, while senior management gives input and support.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam questions often swap these two parties. Board approval keeps the function independent of the managers it reviews; management's support makes the mandate work.
how_it_works: The board discusses the right authority, role and responsibilities with the chief audit executive (CAE) and senior management.
The board approves the internal audit charter, which holds the mandate and the scope and types of services.
Senior management gives input on expectations the board should consider, then supports the mandate across the organization and promotes the function's authority.
The board also approves the plan, budget and resource plan, and sets a reporting level that lets the function fulfill the mandate (Standard 6.3).
Both work together so the function can reach the data, records, people and property it needs.
Whether internal auditors are staff or a contracted firm, the board keeps its responsibility to support and oversee the function (Domain III; 2026 Three Lines statement).

rows.label: Mandate
cells: Supplies information and documents it in the charter

rows.label: Plan, budget, resource plan
cells: Discusses them; works with the board on resources

rows.label: Access to records and people
cells: Works with senior management to enable it
Works with the board and other managers to enable it

rows.label: Recognition of the function
cells: Provides the information needed to promote it

subtopics.example: At a Canadian credit union, the executive team 'signs off' a narrower audit scope that leaves out lending. Simran, a new senior internal auditor, sees that the board never approved the change and tells the CAE, who takes the scope back to the board.

review: Inspect board minutes for the vote approving the charter and its scope
Compare who signed the charter with who the Standards say approves it
evidence: Signed, dated charter showing the approving body
Correspondence recording what senior management asked internal audit to cover
audit_focus.recommend: Route every request to narrow or widen audit coverage through the board's approval process, whichever manager makes it.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes; senior management is consulted beforehand

subtopics.isaca_rule: The board approves; senior management gives input and support. Where several bodies govern, the board is the one empowered to give internal audit its mandate; where none does, whoever governs at the top, such as the organization's head. Must: the CAE discusses the charter with both.

exam_traps.trap: The charter is approved by senior management and the board together.
exam_traps.why: The CAE discusses the charter with both, and the board alone approves it. Even the older text left final approval with the board.

exam_traps.trap: Senior management has no part in the mandate, because involving it would harm independence.
exam_traps.why: Senior management's input is an essential condition (something internal audit needs from it), and its support makes the mandate effective. Input is not approval.

key_terms.definition: The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.
The list of engagements internal audit intends to carry out in a period, chosen by risk.
The plan for the people, money and technology the audit plan needs.

subtopics.memory_aid: The CAE drafts, both discuss, the board approves, senior management supports.

subtopics.name: Essential Conditions and Disagreements
subtopics.definition: Essential conditions are what Domain III, on governing the internal audit function, says the board and senior management need to do; they are not requirements on the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The Standards bind internal auditors, not board members. A chief audit executive (CAE) cannot order a board to act; the duty is to discuss, explain and document.
how_it_works: The CAE must discuss Domain III with the board and senior management, and should cover what internal audit loses without their support.
If either disagrees with a condition, the CAE must show, with examples, how its absence may harm the function, and should suggest alternatives.
If all agree a condition is not needed, the reasons and the substitute conditions must be documented.
If the CAE rejects their reasons, internal audit may be unable to say it fully follows the Standards.
The CAE should then document those reasons, share them with both, and make them available to the external assessor, the outside reviewer of internal audit.
subtopics.example: Joon-ho is CAE of a Korean manufacturer whose board chair refuses private sessions without the chief executive officer. Joon-ho explains, with examples, how matters about senior management could go unreported, and offers an alternative: a standing slot with the audit committee chair alone. The board accepts, and Joon-ho documents the reasons and the alternative condition.

review: Compare each Domain III essential condition with what the board actually does
Inspect the file kept for the external assessor on conditions not provided
evidence: Agenda and minutes of the meeting where Domain III was presented
Signed memo listing each waived condition and its substitute
audit_focus.recommend: Get written confirmation from the board and senior management of which conditions they provide and which substitutes apply.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management decide whether to provide the condition

subtopics.isaca_rule: Board duties are essential conditions, not rules the CAE can enforce. Must: show the impact of a missing one with examples, and document an agreed substitute. Should: suggest alternatives, and document an unresolved disagreement.

exam_traps.trap: The Standards require the board to approve the charter, so a board that refuses is violating the Standards.
exam_traps.why: The Standards place requirements on internal auditors only. The CAE's requirement is to discuss the conditions and explain what their absence does.

exam_traps.trap: If the board rejects a condition, the CAE should quietly accept it.
exam_traps.why: Silence is not an option. The CAE must explain the impact with examples, and should offer alternatives and document the reasons if no agreement is reached.

key_terms.definition: Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
A substitute arrangement that makes up for an absent essential condition.

topics.overview: The internal audit charter is the formal document that holds the mandate. This topic covers the minimum content the Standards require, why the chief audit executive discusses the draft with the board and senior management, and why approval belongs to the board.
can_do: Recognize the four items every charter must contain
Tell required charter content from optional topics and from items that are not charter content
Explain why the draft goes to both the board and senior management for discussion
Recognize who approves the charter and why that matters for independence

subtopics.name: Required Charter Content
subtopics.definition: The internal audit charter is the formal document that records the function's mandate, position, reporting lines, scope and types of service.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The charter is the first place to look when someone questions the function's right to act. A missing element, such as the reporting line, leaves a gap.
how_it_works: First, the charter states the Purpose of Internal Auditing (Standard 6.2 Internal Audit Charter).
Second, it commits the function to the Global Internal Audit Standards. Another set, from law or choice, adds to this, never replaces it; the stricter rule may be followed.
Third, it sets out the mandate, with scope and types of services, plus the board's responsibilities and expectations about management's support.
Fourth, it gives the function's organizational position and reporting relationships.
Where they apply, it must also hold the mandate's legal requirements and any ongoing role the chief audit executive (CAE) has beyond internal auditing, with its safeguards.
Other topics should be considered: handling of impairments, unrestricted access, communication with the board, the audit process, quality assessments, and how budgets are approved.
subtopics.example: Farid, an internal auditor at an Emirati hospital group, reads the draft charter before it goes to the board. It states the purpose, mandate and scope, but says nothing about following the Standards or where the function reports. Farid lists the two missing items and returns the draft to the CAE.

review: Compare the charter against the four minimum items in Standard 6.2
Inspect whether nonaudit roles and their safeguards are written into the charter
evidence: Current charter with the date the board approved it
Checklist mapping charter sections to the required content
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive add the absent sections and bring the revised text to the next board meeting.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves the charter's content

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: the charter states at least four things: the Purpose of Internal Auditing, the commitment to the Standards, the mandate with scope and services, and the organizational position and reporting relationships. Should: consider other topics. The plan and budget are not required.

exam_traps.trap: The charter must contain the internal audit plan and the budget.
exam_traps.why: Neither is required charter content. The charter may describe how budgets are approved; the plan and budget are separate items.

exam_traps.trap: The charter and the mandate are the same thing.
exam_traps.why: The mandate is the authority, role and responsibilities. The charter is the document that holds it, with the purpose, the Standards commitment and the reporting relationships.

key_terms.definition: Where the function sits in the structure, as set by the board.
The chief audit executive's lines: directly to the board, and administratively to a member of management.
The kinds of work the function offers, such as assurance and advice.

subtopics.memory_aid: Purpose, Standards, mandate, position: the four charter musts.

subtopics.name: Charter Discussion Before Approval
subtopics.definition: Discussing the charter means the chief audit executive (CAE) takes the proposed text to the board and senior management to confirm it matches what they understand and expect.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A charter that management has never seen will be resisted in practice, and one the board does not understand may not be approved. Discussion builds the shared understanding that later makes access and cooperation easier.
how_it_works: The CAE develops the charter and keeps it up to date.
Before approval, the proposed charter must be discussed with both the board and senior management (Standard 6.2 Internal Audit Charter).
The aim is to confirm the wording matches what both groups understand and expect of internal audit.
The board is expected to raise other topics the charter should cover to make the function effective.
Senior management is expected to tell the board and the CAE what management expects, so it can be considered for inclusion.
Typically the final draft is presented at a board meeting, discussed there and approved.
subtopics.example: Ngozi, CAE of a Nigerian telecom, drafts a charter that adds advisory services. Before the board meeting, Ngozi walks the chief executive officer and the finance director through the draft and notes their expectations about notice before engagements. Ngozi then presents the final draft to the audit committee, explains management's input, and asks the board to approve it.

review: Trace the draft charter to recorded discussions with senior management and the board
Compare expectations raised in discussion with the final charter wording
evidence: Tracked-changes versions of the charter showing whose comments were adopted
Board papers that summarize senior management's comments on the proposed text
audit_focus.recommend: Record senior management's comments on each draft, and have the chief audit executive show the board how they were handled.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes on the final text

subtopics.isaca_rule: Discuss with both, approve by one. Must: before approval, the CAE takes the proposed charter to the board and senior management for discussion. Then the board approves it.

exam_traps.trap: Discussing the draft with senior management compromises independence, so it should go straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: The Standards require the discussion with both. Hearing management's expectations does not hand management control; the board still decides and approves.

exam_traps.trap: Because senior management reviewed the charter, its sign-off completes the approval.
exam_traps.why: Discussion is not approval. Senior management communicates expectations; the approval belongs to the board.

key_terms.definition: The chief audit executive's draft, taken to the board and senior management for discussion before approval.
What senior management hopes internal audit will cover or how it will work; input the board may weigh.

subtopics.name: Board Approval and Keeping the Charter Current
subtopics.definition: Board approval of the charter is the board's formal adoption of the document that records the mandate; the charter is then reviewed when circumstances change.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A charter the board has adopted cannot be set aside by a manager who dislikes a finding. Approval by anyone lower would make the internal audit function depend on the people it audits.
how_it_works: The board approves the charter (Standard 6.2 Internal Audit Charter, essential conditions). The chief audit executive (CAE) who drafted it does not, and neither does senior management.
Approval shows the board's support and fixes the reporting level the board has determined.
The board reviews the charter with the CAE when things change, such as a new CAE or a shift in the organization's risks.
The CAE and the board should agree how often to review and reaffirm the charter. Periodic review is a leading practice.
Changes to the charter go back to the board for approval.
Where laws or regulations fully cover what a charter must contain, they may stand in for a formal charter.
subtopics.example: At a Polish energy company, the charter was last approved six years ago, before the move into renewable power. When a plant director challenges internal audit's right to review a wind-farm contract, the old charter does not mention that business. Bartek, the engagement supervisor, tells the CAE, who discusses an update with senior management and submits it for board approval.

review: Compare the charter's approval date with changes in leadership, strategy and risks
Inspect whether the agreed review frequency was kept
evidence: Minutes recording the vote on the charter and on each amendment
Calendar entry or policy fixing how often the charter is reaffirmed
audit_focus.recommend: Schedule the next charter check now, and have the chief audit executive tie it to leadership or strategy changes.
audit_focus.decides: The board votes on the original and on every amendment

subtopics.isaca_rule: The board, and nobody below it, approves the charter. Approval by the CAE would be self-approval. Should: agree with the board how often to review the charter. Revisit it when the organization, its risks or the CAE changes.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE approves the charter, being accountable for the function.
exam_traps.why: The CAE develops and maintains it. Approval has to come from above the function, so it belongs to the board.

exam_traps.trap: A charter approved once stays valid until the Standards change.
exam_traps.why: The board reviews it with the CAE when circumstances change, such as a new CAE or new risks.

key_terms.definition: The board's formal decision to adopt the charter, usually recorded in meeting minutes with a date.
To confirm, after review, that the charter still lets the function meet its objectives.

topics.overview: Internal audit gives two kinds of service. Assurance is an objective assessment against criteria that raises confidence. Advisory work is advice with no assurance and no management responsibility. This topic covers both, the two levels of assurance, how advisory scope is agreed, and how to pick the right service.
can_do: Tell an assurance engagement from an advisory engagement in a scenario
Explain what decides whether assurance is limited or reasonable
Explain who settles what an advisory engagement covers, and who sets objectives and scope for assurance
Choose the service that fits a request and name the safeguards that apply

subtopics.name: Assurance Services
subtopics.definition: Assurance services are objective assessments in which internal auditors compare an activity with set criteria and state a conclusion that raises stakeholders' confidence in it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The board and senior management rely on assurance to know whether governance, risk management and control processes work. That reliance is only justified if the internal auditors, not those under review, shaped the work.
how_it_works: Assurance compares the existing condition of governance, risk management and control processes with established criteria; a gap is a potential finding.
The engagement ends in a conclusion on effectiveness, and it says so when processes are working well (Standard 14.5 Engagement Conclusions).
Internal auditors mainly set objectives and scope; the chief audit executive (CAE) or a delegated engagement supervisor approves them.
Internal auditors may change objectives and scope as the work requires. The CAE must approve each change, management must be told promptly, and the scope must suffice for the objectives.
Main users: the board, senior management and management of the activity under review. Examples: technology, compliance, financial, and operational or performance engagements.
subtopics.example: The board of a Kenyan agricultural lender asks whether loan approvals follow the credit policy. Njeri, an internal auditor, sets the objectives and scope, takes the policy as criteria and tests a sample of approved loans against it. Njeri records the gaps as potential findings and drafts a conclusion on whether the approval controls are effective.

review: Compare the condition found with the criteria agreed during planning
Trace each finding and the conclusion to evidence in the workpapers
evidence: Test results obtained directly by the internal auditors
Planning memo naming the yardstick chosen and why it is adequate
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the management of the activity under review for action plans that address the root cause of each finding.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides and carries out the actions; the board oversees

subtopics.isaca_rule: Assurance means criteria, evidence and a conclusion. Internal auditors mainly set the objectives and scope. Must: the CAE approves them, or delegates that to an engagement supervisor and stays accountable; the conclusion states whether processes are effective, including when they are.

exam_traps.trap: The management of the activity under review sets the scope of an assurance engagement.
exam_traps.why: Management's input is considered, but internal auditors mainly set assurance objectives and scope, and the CAE approves them. Otherwise the management under review could steer the result.

exam_traps.trap: An assurance report only matters when it lists problems.
exam_traps.why: When no gap is found, the conclusion still gives assurance that the processes are effective.

key_terms.definition: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
What the internal auditors actually found: the existing state of the activity.
The auditors' overall verdict on the engagement results, taken together.

subtopics.name: Limited and Reasonable Assurance
subtopics.definition: Limited and reasonable assurance are the two levels of assurance the Standards name; which one applies depends on what procedures were done, when, and how much.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Readers act on the level of confidence a report claims. Claiming more than the work supports misleads the board, so the words in the conclusion have to match the procedures behind it.
how_it_works: The Standards glossary names two levels, limited and reasonable assurance, and defines neither.
All it ties the choice to is the nature, timing and extent of the procedures performed.
Nature is the kind of procedure, timing is when, and extent is how much.
Neither level is a guarantee. Assurance is meant to raise confidence, and internal auditors are not expected to be infallible.
A function's methodologies may use a rating scale to show whether reasonable assurance exists on control effectiveness.
The other sense, the reasonable assurance that controls can give management, is in 1C5.1 and 1C8.2.
subtopics.example: Camille, an internal auditor at a French university, is asked for a quick review of research grant spending. Time allows only interviews and a read of the procedures for one month, not testing of transactions across the year. Camille tells the engagement supervisor that the conclusion cannot claim more than this work supports, and words it to say what was and was not tested.

review: Compare the level of assurance stated with the procedures in the work program
Inspect the conclusion for claims the evidence does not support
evidence: Work program listing each test, its sample size and the months covered
Final communication wording on what was and was not examined
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive set out in the methodologies how conclusions describe the work behind them.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive approves the final communication

subtopics.isaca_rule: The level of assurance follows the work done: its nature, timing and extent. The Standards name limited and reasonable assurance without defining them. Assurance raises confidence; it is never a guarantee.

exam_traps.trap: Reasonable assurance means the internal auditors guarantee there are no errors or fraud.
exam_traps.why: Assurance is a statement meant to raise confidence, not a promise. The Standards also say internal auditors exercising due professional care are not expected to be infallible.

exam_traps.trap: Every internal audit assurance engagement gives reasonable assurance.
exam_traps.why: The glossary says internal auditors may give limited or reasonable assurance. Which one depends on the nature, timing and extent of the procedures performed, not on habit or on who asked.

key_terms.definition: The kind of work done, such as interviews, inspection of records or direct testing.
When the work is done and which period it covers.
How much is examined, such as the size of a sample or a whole population.

subtopics.name: Advisory Services and How Their Scope Is Agreed
subtopics.definition: Advisory services are internal auditors' advice to stakeholders, given without providing assurance and without taking on management responsibilities.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Advisory work lets internal audit help before problems occur. The risk is drifting from adviser to decision maker, which would damage objectivity and any later assurance.
how_it_works: Advisory work can begin with the internal auditors' own suggestion or a request from the board, senior management or an activity's management (Domain V introduction).
Nature and scope are agreed with the requesting party; objectives and scope are typically set jointly.
The work program should be developed with the stakeholders who asked.
Depending on that agreement, a formal documented risk assessment, evaluation criteria and evidence-based findings may not be needed.

Required whatever is agreed: objectivity, competency, due professional care, approval of objectives and scope, and (a must) documenting and communicating a significant risk as a finding (Standard 14.3).
The board should also know of advisory work under way (Three Lines Model).
subtopics.example: A Singapore shipping firm's procurement head asks internal audit for advice on a draft supplier onboarding policy. Internal auditor Wei Ling agrees the scope: comment on control gaps, no testing, no sign-off. With the chief audit executive's approval, Wei Ling sends written suggestions, leaves procurement to choose which to adopt, and records that the work gave advice, not assurance.

review: Compare the agreed advisory scope with the work actually performed
Inspect advisory files for decisions taken by internal auditors instead of management
evidence: Signed terms of the engagement, stating what is in and out
Sign-off sheet showing who authorized the engagement to start
audit_focus.recommend: Make clear in the file that the requesting managers own every decision and that internal audit only advised.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides what to adopt from the advice

subtopics.isaca_rule: Advisory work is advice without assurance and without management responsibility. Its nature and scope are agreed with the requesting party, and management makes every decision. The Standards still apply unless a standard says otherwise. Should: build the work program with the requester.

exam_traps.trap: Advisory work is informal, so the Standards do not apply to it.
exam_traps.why: The Standards apply to assurance and advisory work alike, except where an individual standard says otherwise. Only specific items, such as a formal risk assessment, may be unnecessary.

exam_traps.trap: Because management asked for help, the auditor can make the design decision for them.
exam_traps.why: Advice stops short of deciding. Taking on management responsibility impairs objectivity and blocks credible assurance later.

key_terms.definition: The stakeholder who asks for an advisory service and agrees its nature and scope.
Deciding, approving, implementing or owning a process or control. It stays with management in every engagement.
Specialist fact-finding on records and data; the Standards list it as an example of advisory services.

subtopics.name: Choosing the Right Service
subtopics.definition: Choosing the service means deciding, from what the stakeholder needs and what the charter allows, whether an engagement should give assurance or advice.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Expectations and requirements differ between the two services. A wrong label leaves the board believing it has assurance it never received.
how_it_works: Ask what is needed: confidence that something works against criteria (assurance), or input to improve or design something (advisory).
Without adequate criteria, internal auditors must settle suitable ones in discussion with the board, senior management or both; this may lead to advisory work.
A request to swap a planned assurance engagement for advisory work is a conflicting demand that the chief audit executive (CAE) reports to the board and senior management.
Assurance may follow advisory work in the same area only if the CAE confirms objectivity is not impaired and staffs the engagement to manage it (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity).

Internal auditors must not assess activities they were once responsible for; within 12 months, objectivity is presumed impaired for assurance. Advising is allowed after disclosure to the requesting party.

rows.label: What is delivered
cells: A conclusion against criteria that raises confidence

rows.label: Risk assessment, criteria, findings
cells: May not be needed, depending on the agreement

rows.label: Topical Requirements
cells: Mandatory when the topic is in scope

subtopics.example: A logistics company in Mexico plans a new warehouse system. The operations director asks the internal audit function to 'audit' the design, but no approved requirements exist to test against and the director mainly wants ideas on controls. Ximena, the internal auditor, concludes that advice fits better, explains that no assurance will be given, and notes that later assurance must be staffed to protect objectivity.

review: Compare each engagement's label with what was actually delivered
Trace assurance engagements that followed advisory work to the objectivity confirmation
evidence: Planning records stating which of the two services is intended
Staffing sheet showing who advised earlier and who now tests
audit_focus.recommend: Bring each proposal to trade a planned audit for advice to the board first, through the chief audit executive.
audit_focus.decides: The board approves significant changes to the internal audit plan

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: consider whether an engagement gives assurance (confidence against criteria) or advice (input on something being built or improved). Must: before assurance follows advice, the CAE confirms objectivity is not impaired. Who may staff the engagement is covered in 1B2.4.

exam_traps.trap: Once internal audit has advised on an area, it can never audit that area.
exam_traps.why: It can, if the CAE confirms the earlier advice does not impair objectivity and staffs the engagement accordingly.

exam_traps.trap: Management asked for an audit, so the engagement must be assurance.
exam_traps.why: The label follows the need and the work. With no criteria to test against and a request for ideas, advice fits, and no assurance is claimed.

key_terms.definition: Competing requests for internal audit's time, reported to the board and senior management.
Whether an engagement gives assurance or advice; it decides which requirements apply.

subtopics.memory_aid: Confidence against criteria: assurance. Help while building: advisory.

topics.overview: Assurance engagements come in several kinds, named for what they examine. This topic describes each kind the syllabus lists, what it looks at and why, so you can match a scenario to the right engagement.
can_do: Describe what each kind of assurance engagement examines
Tell an operational audit from a compliance audit and from a financial audit
Explain why access rights in a contract matter for work on third parties
Describe what an audit of culture and an audit of management reporting look at

subtopics.name: Risk and Control Assessments
subtopics.definition: A risk and control assessment is an assurance engagement that asks whether the controls over an activity's significant risks are well designed and working.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Almost every assurance engagement has this logic at its core: objective, risk, control. Knowing it lets you place the other engagement types as variations with a narrower focus.
how_it_works: The internal auditors first understand the activity's objectives, then identify the risks that could stop those objectives being met.
Risks are ranked by significance, usually by impact and likelihood, and the most significant are reviewed first.
For the most significant risks, assessing control design first helps decide which controls are worth testing for operation.
Controls tested typically deal with authority and responsibility, compliance, reliable reporting, efficient use of resources and safeguarding of assets.
A risk and control matrix may be used to link objectives, risks and controls.
Fraud risks are considered in every engagement risk assessment (Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment).
subtopics.example: Catalina, an internal auditor at a pharmacy chain in Chile, reviews controlled-drug inventory. Catalina confirms the objective (drugs are accounted for), lists the risks (theft, miscounts), and maps the controls (locked storage, dual counts). The dual count looks well designed, so Catalina tests whether two people really sign each count. Catalina records the results in a risk and control matrix and drafts the findings.

review: Walk the process to confirm how each key control is meant to work
Evaluate control design before sampling transactions to test operation
Compare the remaining risk with the organization's risk tolerance, where established
evidence: Reperformance and inspection results the audit team produced itself
Process narrative or flowchart confirmed by the people who run it
audit_focus.recommend: Ask process managers to redesign controls that cannot manage the risk and repair those that do not operate.
audit_focus.decides: Management chooses the risk response within the organization's risk appetite

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: understand the activity, assess its significant risks and consider fraud risk. May: judge control design first, the order the considerations describe. Management owns the risks and the controls; internal auditors assess them.

exam_traps.trap: Test how the controls operate first; design can be looked at if time allows.
exam_traps.why: A badly designed control cannot manage the risk even if it runs perfectly. Assessing design first shows which controls are worth testing.

exam_traps.trap: The internal auditors decide which risks the activity should accept.
exam_traps.why: The auditors assess and report. Management decides how to respond to risks, within the appetite and tolerance the organization has set.

key_terms.definition: A working table that lines up objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them.
Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
Whether a control actually works as designed, consistently, over the period.

subtopics.name: Operational, Financial, Compliance, Performance and Quality Audits
subtopics.definition: Operational, financial and compliance audits are the classic assurance engagements; each tests one kind of objective: efficient operations, reliable financial information, or adherence to rules.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Exam scenarios describe what the internal auditors are checking and ask you to name the engagement. The quickest route is to ask which objective is being tested.
how_it_works: Each kind is named for the objective it tests; the engagement steps stay the same.
The Standards glossary gives engagements on compliance, financial matters, operations or performance, and technology as examples of assurance services.
Four risk areas run through them: reliable financial and operational information, effective and efficient operations, safeguarding of assets, and compliance with laws and regulations.
One engagement can combine kinds, such as an operational audit that also tests a safety regulation. Must (Standard 13.3): objectives cover any goal a law or regulation mandates.
Internal audit's financial work serves the board and management. The external auditor's opinion on the financial statements serves outside stakeholders and sits outside the three lines.

types.meaning: Examines how effectively and efficiently an operation or program achieves its objectives.
Asks how well an activity or program achieves its goals. The Standards glossary lists operational and performance engagements together.
Examines the reliability and integrity of financial information and the controls that produce it.
Checks adherence to the laws and regulations that apply to the organization.
In general terms, checks whether a product, service or process meets the quality requirements set for it. The Standards do not define this engagement.

subtopics.example: A Vietnamese garment maker asks internal audit to review its cutting department. Thuy, the internal auditor, is told to find out why fabric waste is above target and whether machine time is well used. No law or policy is being tested, and no financial figures are being verified. Thuy identifies the work as an operational audit and takes the department's waste and output targets as criteria.

review: Identify the objective under test before choosing criteria and procedures
Compare actual results with the targets, rules or records that serve as criteria
evidence: Production, cost and quality data extracted by the audit team
The statute, license condition or internal rule being tested against
audit_focus.recommend: Agree with the management of the activity how it will close each gap between results and criteria, starting from its root cause.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the operation and decides how to improve it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Name the engagement by the objective tested: efficiency and effectiveness is operational, adherence to a rule is compliance, reliability of financial information is financial. Internal audit's financial work is not the external auditor's opinion.

exam_traps.trap: An audit that asks whether a process is efficient is a compliance audit, because the process has procedures.
exam_traps.why: Compliance audits test adherence to a rule. When the question is how well resources are used or goals are met, the engagement is operational or performance.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit's financial audit gives the opinion on the financial statements.
exam_traps.why: That opinion comes from the external auditor and serves outside parties. Internal audit gives the board and management assurance on financial information and its controls.

key_terms.definition: Meeting the binding rules that apply: law, regulation, contract and the organization's own policies.
An outside firm that gives an independent opinion, mainly on financial statements, for stakeholders outside the organization.

subtopics.name: Third-Party, Contract Compliance, IT Security and Privacy Audits
subtopics.definition: Third-party, contract compliance, IT security and privacy audits are assurance engagements over risks that sit with outside parties, information systems and personal data.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An organization stays accountable even when a supplier does the work or a system holds the data. These audits tell the board whether those exposures are governed and controlled.
how_it_works: A third-party audit looks at how the organization selects, contracts, onboards, monitors and exits its suppliers and other outside parties.
A contract compliance audit checks whether the parties are meeting a contract's terms.
Access matters: if the contract has no right-to-audit clause, the internal audit function may be unable to examine the third party directly and its assurance may be restricted.
An IT security audit looks at how the organization governs, risk-manages and controls the protection of its systems and data.
A privacy audit checks how personal information is protected and whether privacy laws, regulations and policies are followed.
A Topical Requirement applies when its topic is planned, arises in an engagement or is requested; every requirement is assessed, each exclusion's reason documented.
subtopics.example: A Philippine bank outsources card printing. Jun, an internal auditor, plans to visit the printer's site to test how card data is protected, but the contract has no right-to-audit clause and the printer declines. Jun reports the restriction to the engagement supervisor, asks for the printer's independent assurance report instead, and recommends adding audit rights at renewal.

review: Inspect key contracts for audit rights and for security and privacy terms
Compare the supplier's actual performance with the contract terms
Evaluate management's ongoing monitoring of high-risk third parties
evidence: Service-level and incident data for the supplier, obtained directly
Signed agreements with their security and data protection schedules
Complete list of third-party relationships ranked by risk
audit_focus.recommend: Advise contract owners to negotiate audit rights into high-risk agreements and to review supplier performance on a set schedule.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the third-party relationship and its risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Outsourcing moves the work, not the accountability. Internal audit assesses how management governs and controls third parties, systems and personal data. Must: follow a Topical Requirement in force for assurance on its topic; for advisory work it is recommended.

exam_traps.trap: A contract compliance audit can always go ahead, because internal audit has unrestricted access.
exam_traps.why: The charter grants access inside the organization. Access to a third party's records depends on the contract; without a right-to-audit clause, assurance may be limited.

exam_traps.trap: Once a process is outsourced, its risks belong to the supplier.
exam_traps.why: The hiring organization keeps accountability for risks to its objectives. Management must still govern, monitor and control the relationship.

key_terms.definition: An outside person or entity that supplies the organization with products or services, such as a vendor or contractor.
A contract term that lets the organization or its auditors examine a third party's records and controls.

subtopics.name: Culture and Management Reporting Audits
subtopics.definition: Audits of culture and of management reporting are assurance engagements over two things that shape every decision: how people behave and what information leaders receive.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls on paper fail when behavior works against them, and boards decide badly on unreliable reports. 1C2.1 defines culture and tone; 1D4.1 links them to fraud.
how_it_works: An audit of culture examines whether behavior in the organization supports its objectives and ethical expectations.
It treats behavior like any other risk: are the governance, risk management and control processes over it designed well and working?
Typical subjects are the tone leaders set, incentives, speak-up channels such as hotlines, training, and how misconduct is handled.
Evidence mixes numbers and narrative: survey results, complaint and staff turnover data, interviews and observation.
An audit of management reporting examines how management's reports are produced: where the data comes from, how it is compiled and how it is reviewed.
The question is whether decision makers receive accurate, reliable financial and operational information.
subtopics.example: After a mis-selling scandal at a rival, the board of an Australian insurer asks for assurance on sales culture. Mele, an internal auditor, does not rely on the staff survey alone. Mele reviews how bonuses are set, reads complaint and speak-up data, and interviews branch teams about pressure to sell, then reports the gaps against the code of conduct to the chief audit executive.

review: Compare incentive schemes with the behavior the organization says it expects
Trace a sample of board report figures back to source data
Evaluate how concerns raised by staff are investigated and escalated
evidence: Reconciliations of reported figures to source systems, reperformed by the audit team
Exit interview themes, disciplinary records and hotline case logs
audit_focus.recommend: Encourage senior management to align incentives and reporting controls with the behavior and accuracy the board expects.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management set expectations for behavior

subtopics.isaca_rule: Culture can be audited: assess the processes that shape behavior, using several kinds of evidence. Must: the internal audit plan responds to changes in organizational culture. For management reporting, assess the process behind the numbers, not only one report.

exam_traps.trap: A culture audit is a staff satisfaction survey run by the internal audit function.
exam_traps.why: A survey is one source of evidence. The engagement assesses governance, risk management and control over behavior, such as tone, incentives and how concerns are handled.

exam_traps.trap: Culture is too soft to give assurance on.
exam_traps.why: Behavior leaves evidence: incentives, complaints, turnover, decisions. Standard 9.4 Internal Audit Plan expects the plan to respond to changes in organizational culture.

key_terms.definition: How people in an organization actually behave and work together, and what drives that behavior.
The visible side of culture: what people actually do at work and how they deal with one another. 'The way we do things'.

topics.overview: Advisory work takes many forms, from training to advice on a new system. This topic describes the internal auditor's role in each kind the syllabus lists and the line that role must not cross: advise and facilitate, never decide, approve or own.
can_do: Describe the internal auditor's part in each kind of advisory work
Tell advising on a design from approving or owning it
Explain what must happen before assurance is given on an area internal audit advised on
Describe how benchmarking and process mapping help management

subtopics.name: Risk and Control Training and Internal Control Assessments
subtopics.definition: Risk and control training and facilitated control assessments are advisory services in which internal auditors teach and guide while managers assess and own their own controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Managers who understand risk and control run better processes between audits. The danger is the auditor ending up as the author of management's assessment, and later auditing their own conclusions.
how_it_works: The Standards glossary lists training, and leading discussions on risk and control, among its examples of advisory services.
In training the auditor explains risk and control and management applies them; owning the program is a role beyond internal auditing (KaiSip's reading).
In a control self-assessment, managers and staff judge their own risks and controls. It is a first-line activity.
The internal auditor may facilitate the workshop, supply a method, ask probing questions and challenge assumptions.
The ratings, the conclusions and the action plans belong to management, not to the facilitator.
Later assurance may draw on the results, but only after the auditors judge how far that work can be relied on.
subtopics.example: At a Dutch food distributor, the internal audit function ran a workshop on warehouse risks and, to save time, the auditor typed in the final ratings. A year later the same team was asked to audit the warehouse and found itself reviewing its own scores. Femke, the new engagement supervisor, asks the warehouse managers to set and sign their own ratings, and records internal audit's part as facilitator only.

review: Inspect session records for who made each scoring decision
Compare training content with the risks the trained teams actually face
evidence: Attendance lists and scored worksheets signed by the participating managers
Engagement terms describing internal audit's part in the sessions
audit_focus.recommend: Have line management sign the self-assessment results and track the resulting actions to completion.
audit_focus.decides: Line managers decide the scores and the follow-up

subtopics.isaca_rule: Teach and facilitate; do not assess for them. In training and control self-assessment the internal auditor brings method and challenge, while management owns the ratings, the conclusions and the actions.

exam_traps.trap: Because internal audit ran the workshop, the control self-assessment results are internal audit's assurance.
exam_traps.why: Facilitating is advisory work and gives no assurance. The assessment is management's own, and any later assurance needs the auditors' own evaluation.

exam_traps.trap: Training managers on controls impairs independence, so auditors should decline.
exam_traps.why: Training is a recognized advisory service. Objectivity is kept by not taking on management responsibility, not by refusing to share knowledge.

key_terms.definition: A process in which managers and staff evaluate the risks and controls in their own area.
The person who guides a session and its method without owning its conclusions.
Work done by operational management, which owns and manages risk day to day.

subtopics.name: Advising on System Design, Due Diligence and Data Privacy
subtopics.definition: Advising on system design, due diligence and data privacy means giving management risk and control input on a new system, a planned deal or personal data handling.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Building a control in is cheaper than adding it later. Early advice is valuable as long as decisions stay with management.
how_it_works: In system design and development, the internal auditor advises on risks and controls while the system is designed and built.
The auditor may sit on a project committee as an adviser, but should not take part in its decisions.
The auditor does not design, approve, sign off or implement the system or its controls.
In due diligence before a major deal or new third-party relationship, the auditor may advise on the target's risks and controls. Management decides whether to proceed.
On data privacy, the auditor advises on privacy risks and whether planned controls meet laws and policies. A manager owns the privacy program.
If assurance on the same area follows, the chief audit executive (CAE) must confirm objectivity is not impaired and assign staff to manage it (Standard 2.2 Safeguarding Objectivity).
subtopics.example: A Saudi retailer is building a loyalty app that stores customers' personal data. Reem, an internal auditor, joins the project steering committee as a non-voting adviser. Reem notes that the design lacks consent records and access logging, and suggests options. Asked by the project manager to approve the final design, Reem declines, explains that approval is management's, and documents the advice given.

review: Inspect project minutes for any vote or approval by an internal auditor
Compare the advice given with the scope agreed for the advisory engagement
evidence: Committee terms of reference listing members with and without a vote
Written memo of suggestions sent to the sponsor, with the reply
audit_focus.recommend: Obtain the project sponsor's signature on the design, with a record of how the internal audit function's suggestions were handled.
audit_focus.decides: Management approves the design and decides whether a deal proceeds

subtopics.isaca_rule: Advise early, decide never. The internal auditor gives input on risks and controls; management designs, approves and owns. Must: before later assurance on that area, the CAE confirms objectivity is not impaired.

exam_traps.trap: Signing off the controls in a new system is the most useful help internal audit can give.
exam_traps.why: Sign-off is a management decision. An auditor who approves the design has taken management responsibility and cannot later assess it objectively.

exam_traps.trap: As a steering committee member, the internal auditor should vote like everyone else.
exam_traps.why: The auditor contributes questions and insight as an adviser. Taking part in decisions would put the auditor in management's seat.

key_terms.definition: A careful investigation of a company, partner or supplier before entering a deal or relationship.
Losing a critical eye when assessing work one designed, decided or performed oneself.

subtopics.name: Benchmarking and Process Mapping
subtopics.definition: Benchmarking and process mapping are advisory tools: one compares an activity with others to find better practice, the other draws how a process flows from start to finish.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Managers often cannot see their own process whole or know how peers perform. A comparison or a map gives them a factual base for improvement decisions that remain theirs.
how_it_works: Internal benchmarking compares the same measure across areas of the organization.
External benchmarking compares the organization's information with that of similar organizations.
The internal auditor gathers comparable data, explains the differences and points to practices worth considering.
A process map, flowchart or narrative shows each step, who performs it, and where decisions and handoffs occur.
Mapping reveals where risks arise and where controls sit, are missing or duplicated.
The same tools serve assurance work: benchmarks can be criteria, and maps help auditors understand an activity.
subtopics.example: The head of customer service at an Indian telecom asks why complaints take so long to close. Arjun, an internal auditor, maps the complaint process with the team and finds three handoffs with no owner. Arjun also compares closing times across the company's four regional centers and shares what the fastest center does differently. Arjun presents the map and the comparison and leaves the choice of changes to the head of customer service.

review: Walk the mapped process with the people who perform each step
Compare like with like before drawing conclusions from benchmark data
evidence: Flowchart signed as accurate by the manager accountable for it
Benchmark data with its source and the period covered
audit_focus.recommend: Leave it to the accountable manager to assign each unowned step and choose which comparison findings to act on.
audit_focus.decides: The manager accountable for the process, not the internal audit function

subtopics.isaca_rule: Benchmarking and mapping give management facts, not instructions. The internal auditor compares, draws and explains; the process owner decides what to change and owns the process. May: internal auditors can propose this work themselves; its nature and scope are still agreed with the manager first (1A4.3).

exam_traps.trap: After mapping the process, internal audit should redesign it and roll out the new version.
exam_traps.why: Redesign and rollout are management's work. The auditor's map and suggestions are advice; owning the change would be a management responsibility.

exam_traps.trap: A benchmark shows what the organization must do.
exam_traps.why: A benchmark is a comparison, not a rule. Differences in size, risk and strategy matter, so management weighs the result before acting.

key_terms.definition: Comparing performance between units or sites inside one organization.
Comparing performance with similar organizations or recognized good practice.
A diagram of a process's steps, people and decision points, from start to finish.
The manager accountable for how a process is designed and performs.

topics.overview: Independence belongs to the internal audit function and comes from where it sits. This topic covers the reporting lines that protect or threaten it, what the board and the chief audit executive each do to guard it, and what happens when budgets, scope or access are restricted. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Identify reporting arrangements that impair the function's independence
Describe what the board does to protect independence
Describe what the chief audit executive must confirm, disclose and document
Identify the right response to a budget cut, a scope limitation or restricted access

subtopics.name: Independence and the Reporting Lines
subtopics.definition: Independence is the internal audit function's freedom from conditions that could bias its work; it rests on a direct reporting line to the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: If the people being audited control the internal auditors' boss, pay or access, findings can be softened or buried. A direct line to the board prevents that.
how_it_works: The chief audit executive (CAE) reports directly to the board, the functional line: the function answers to the board, not management, for its work.
For day-to-day administration, the CAE often reports to a manager: the administrative line.
Reporting administratively to the chief executive officer is a leading practice. Another senior officer may work with safeguards (Standard 7.1, considerations).
If the functional line runs to a manager, or the board cannot be reached directly, independence is not supported.
Another threat: assurance over an area run by the administrative boss, when that boss is not the chief executive officer.
Heads of internal audit in subsidiaries, branches or divisions should have direct access to the senior managers who run those units (Standard 7.1, considerations).

rows.label: Reports to
cells: A member of management, ideally the chief executive officer

rows.label: Typical matters
cells: Charter, plan, budget approval, results, appointment and removal
Day-to-day matters such as expenses and human resources administration

rows.label: Why it exists
cells: Lets the function work and report without interference
Gives access to senior management and the standing to challenge it

rows.label: Main threat
cells: Missing or weak: independence is not supported
Auditing areas run by an administrative boss below the chief executive officer

subtopics.example: At a Turkish construction group, the CAE reports only to the chief operating officer, who sits in on every audit committee meeting. Assigned to audit logistics, which reports to the same officer, internal auditor Deniz raises the concern with the CAE, who discloses the impairment to the board and proposes safeguards.

review: Compare the actual reporting lines with those documented in the charter
List audits of units that report to the same executive as internal audit does
evidence: Calendar invitations and minutes of meetings held with board members
Organization chart and charter showing both reporting lines
audit_focus.recommend: Disclose the reporting-line threat to the board through the chief audit executive, and agree safeguards for the affected engagements.
audit_focus.decides: The board determines the function's reporting relationships and positioning

subtopics.isaca_rule: Functional reporting to the board supports independence. Administrative reporting to the chief executive officer is a leading practice, not a requirement. The line becomes a threat when it blocks access to the board, or when internal audit audits areas run by an administrative boss below the chief executive officer.

exam_traps.trap: Reporting administratively to the chief financial officer always breaches the Standards.
exam_traps.why: Another senior officer is allowed with safeguards. The threat is assurance over that officer's own areas, or lost access to the board.

exam_traps.trap: An auditor with a personal conflict has an independence problem.
exam_traps.why: That is the person's objectivity (see 1B2.1), disclosed to the CAE or a designated supervisor. Independence is the function's, raised by the CAE with the board and senior management.

key_terms.definition: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to do and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence.

subtopics.name: How the Board Protects Independence
subtopics.definition: Board protection of independence is the set of board actions, listed as essential conditions, that place the internal audit function beyond management's control.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The chief audit executive (CAE) cannot protect independence alone, because pressure usually comes from more senior people. Only the board can stand behind the function.
how_it_works: The board sets a direct line to the CAE, requires positioning free of management interference, and asks whether scope, access, authority or resources are restricted.
The board authorizes the CAE's appointment and removal, with senior management's input (Standard 7.1); if the post falls vacant, it should name an interim head or heads (Domain III).
On the CAE's performance evaluation and pay, the board only gives input to senior management.
The board meets the CAE without senior management present: at least yearly as a consideration, quarterly as a leading practice.
A private session is a channel, not a secret: the CAE should tell senior management what was discussed unless inappropriate, and must share how resource limits affect coverage.
Must (Standard 7.2): the CAE helps the board understand, with information and examples, what qualifications a CAE needs. The board approves the role; a succession plan is a should.
subtopics.example: A Colombian utility's chief executive wants to dismiss the CAE over a critical contract report. Valentina, a senior internal auditor, explains that removal needs the board's authorization and that the CAE can raise it privately with the audit committee.

review: Inspect minutes for the resolution that hired or dismissed the chief audit executive
Confirm private sessions without senior management present actually took place
evidence: Attendance records of closed meetings, showing who was in the room
Human resources file showing who contributed to the appraisal and salary review
audit_focus.recommend: Raise any missing protection with the board and document the outcome; the chief audit executive leads that discussion.
audit_focus.decides: The board holds the hiring and dismissal decision

subtopics.isaca_rule: The board protects independence through essential conditions: the direct reporting line, authorizing the CAE's appointment and removal, private sessions (at least yearly is a should) and asking about restrictions. On pay and evaluation the board gives input; it does not set them.

exam_traps.trap: The board sets the CAE's pay.
exam_traps.why: The board gives input to senior management on evaluation and pay; it authorizes appointment and removal.

exam_traps.trap: The CAE must line up a successor.
exam_traps.why: A succession plan is a should; the must is helping the board understand the qualifications the role needs.

key_terms.definition: A meeting of the board and the chief audit executive with no senior management in the room.
The board's decision power over who becomes, and who stops being, chief audit executive.
Acts that hinder the function, such as withholding information or restricting access to people, records or property.

subtopics.name: The Chief Audit Executive's Duties to Confirm, Disclose and Safeguard
subtopics.definition: The chief audit executive's independence duties are to confirm the function's independence to the board at least yearly and to disclose and manage anything that impairs it.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Boards cannot protect what they are not told about. A yearly confirmation plus prompt disclosure of incidents lets the board act before an impairment damages the credibility of internal audit's results.
how_it_works: At least once a year, the chief audit executive (CAE) must confirm the function's organizational independence to the board (Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence).
The confirmation also covers any incident that may have impaired independence, and what was done about it.
Current or proposed roles that could impair independence, in fact or appearance, must be discussed with the board and senior management, with advice on safeguards.
A role beyond internal auditing needs safeguards in the charter and assurance from an independent party; the rules for ongoing and temporary roles are in 1A8.4.
If the governing structure does not support independence, the CAE documents what limits it and any safeguards.
subtopics.example: Hamid, CAE of a Moroccan port operator, prepares the yearly independence confirmation for the board. During the year the procurement head held back contract files for two engagements, and Hamid was asked to vote on a tender committee. Hamid lists both incidents and what was done: access restored after escalation, the vote declined. Hamid then confirms that the direct reporting line to the board is working.

review: Inspect the latest independence statement given to the board and its list of incidents
Trace each nonaudit role to charter wording, safeguards and outside assurance
evidence: Contract with the external firm covering areas the internal audit function cannot review
Board minutes recording receipt of the statement and discussion of incidents
audit_focus.recommend: Keep a log of incidents and nonaudit duties, and have the chief audit executive present it at each board meeting.
audit_focus.decides: The board agrees to each extra duty and its protections

subtopics.isaca_rule: Must: the CAE confirms independence to the board at least yearly, incidents included, and discusses roles that may impair it with the board and senior management. The safeguards a role beyond internal auditing must have are in 1A8.4.

exam_traps.trap: An independence impairment is disclosed to senior management, who decide whether the board needs to know.
exam_traps.why: The confirmation and the incidents go to the board, and they cover impairments in fact or in appearance. Management does not filter the message.
