key_terms.definition: A measure that manages an actual, potential or perceived impairment to independence or objectivity, such as reassignment, outside oversight or outside assurance.
A responsibility the chief audit executive holds beyond internal auditing, such as compliance or risk management.

subtopics.name: Budget Limits, Scope Limitations and Restricted Access
subtopics.definition: Budget limits, scope limitations and restricted access are constraints that stop the internal audit function from doing the work its charter and plan call for.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Nobody needs to forbid an audit to stop it. Starving the budget, narrowing the scope or withholding records does the same more quietly, so the Standards send these matters to the board.
how_it_works: Cutting the budget so far that the function cannot do what its charter requires may impair independence.
The chief audit executive (CAE) reports a budget shortfall's impact promptly to the board, which approves the budget, and to senior management, with a strategy to obtain resources.
A scope limitation is an assurance engagement condition, such as a resource constraint or restricted access, that prevents work the program expected.
Internal auditors discuss a scope limitation with management when it is identified, aiming to resolve it. If that fails, the CAE elevates it to the board.
The final communication of the assurance engagement explains any scope limitation (Standard 15.1 Final Engagement Communication).
subtopics.example: During a payroll audit at an Irish hospital trust, the human resources director refuses Siobhan, the internal auditor, access to executive pay records, calling them confidential. Siobhan discusses the restriction with the director, citing the charter, but it is not lifted. Siobhan documents the scope limitation and reports it to the CAE, who elevates it to the board.

review: Compare approved budget and staffing with what the plan requires
Trace each scope limitation from discovery to resolution or escalation
Confirm scope limitations appear in the final communication
evidence: Workpaper notes of who refused what, when, and the reply given
Board minutes showing the matter was raised and what board members asked
Gap analysis of hours needed against hours funded
audit_focus.recommend: Ask senior management to restore the access the charter grants and to instruct staff to cooperate with internal audit.
audit_focus.decides: The board decides whether to intervene with senior management

subtopics.isaca_rule: Two musts. A scope limitation or restricted access in an engagement (Standard 13.3): discuss with management; if unresolved, the CAE elevates it to the board. A budget or resource shortfall (Standards 8.2, 10.1): the CAE promptly tells the board and senior management the impact.

exam_traps.trap: Settle a scope limitation quietly with the manager and leave it out of the report.
exam_traps.why: Discussion with management comes first, but the CAE elevates an unresolved limitation to the board, and the final communication explains scope limitations.

exam_traps.trap: A budget cut follows the scope-limitation ladder: management first, the board only if that fails.
exam_traps.why: That ladder is for a scope limitation. A shortfall's impact goes promptly to the board, which approves the budget, and to senior management.

key_terms.definition: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
A restriction, such as an inadequate budget, that keeps the function from operating effectively.

subtopics.memory_aid: Scope limit: discuss, then elevate. Budget shortfall: tell the board and senior management promptly.

topics.topic_name: Internal audit and the Three Lines Model
topics.overview: The Three Lines Model explains who does what in governance: the board oversees, first-line management owns and manages risk, second-line roles inside management support, monitor and challenge, and internal audit gives independent assurance and advice as the third line. The model comes from The IIA's 2026 Statement of Position, not from the Standards. It is also a CIA Challenge Exam topic.
can_do: Recognize who sits in each line and what the board and senior management do
Tell second-line roles, which are part of management, from the third line's independent assurance
Recognize first-line and second-line duties that would impair internal audit's independence
Name the safeguards needed when internal audit or its head takes on another role

subtopics.name: The Three Lines Model and Its Roles
subtopics.definition: The Three Lines Model is The IIA's description of how the board, management and the internal audit function each contribute assurance and advice so the organization is well governed.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Clear roles prevent gaps where nobody checks a risk and overlaps where the checker is also the doer. Exam questions ask you to place a task with the right party.
how_it_works: The board gives direction and oversight, sets risk appetite and expectations, and delegates authority and resources to management.
Senior management designs the structures and processes to achieve objectives and answers to the board for managing risk.
The first line is operational management, back office included, so support functions such as human resources sit here. It owns risk, designing and operating processes and controls.
The second line is specialist roles focused on risk, such as risk management and compliance, giving expert support, monitoring and challenge to the first line.
The third line is the internal audit function. It gives independent, objective assurance and advice, including over the second line, and reports functionally to the board.
External auditors and regulators serve outside parties and are not among the three lines.
subtopics.example: A fintech in Estonia hires its first risk manager and asks internal audit who now does what. Kristjan, an internal auditor, sets it out: product teams own and control their risks, the risk manager supports and challenges them, and internal audit independently assesses both and reports to the board.

review: Compare documented roles for each line with what people actually do
Identify risks that no line monitors or that two lines duplicate
evidence: Assurance map showing who covers each significant risk
Job descriptions and committee charters for the risk and compliance teams
audit_focus.recommend: Have the board and senior management define, and document, which role owns, monitors and independently assesses each significant risk.
audit_focus.decides: The board and senior management define roles and responsibilities

subtopics.isaca_rule: First-line management owns and manages risk. Second-line roles, also part of management, support, monitor and challenge. Internal audit, the third line, gives independent assurance and advice and reports functionally to the board. External auditors and regulators sit outside the three lines.

exam_traps.trap: The second line is independent in the same way internal audit is.
exam_traps.why: Second-line roles are part of management, even when they report to a board-level committee. The third line's independence rests on its position and its functional line to the board.

exam_traps.trap: The external auditor is the fourth line of the model.
exam_traps.why: The Statement of Position treats external auditors and regulators as providers outside the three lines. They serve external stakeholders.

key_terms.definition: The managers who run the organization's day-to-day activities, front office and back office.
Answers directly to the board, not to management, for its work.

subtopics.memory_aid: First line owns, second line supports and challenges, third line assures.

subtopics.name: Independence Across the Lines and Coordination
subtopics.definition: Independence across the lines differs by design: the first line is not independent, the second is part of management, and the third is positioned independently, reporting functionally to the board.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A board that treats every source of comfort as equally independent will over-trust management's own checks. The internal audit function therefore also gives assurance over the second line.
how_it_works: The first line is not independent, by design: it runs the processes and controls.
The second line is more objective, being separate from operations, but is still part of management and reports to senior management or a board-level committee.
The third line has the highest organizational independence and can report without undue influence from management.
Coordination and reliance reduce duplication and gaps. An assurance map shows who covers which risk (Standard 9.5 Coordination and Reliance).
Internal audit can pull everyone's assurance work into one picture for the board, and may decline to rely on work of poor quality.
Outsourcing does not change the line: outsourced compliance is still second line, and outsourced internal audit is still third line.

rows.label: Who
cells: Specialist functions such as risk and compliance

rows.label: Main job
cells: Owns risk; designs and runs controls

rows.label: Reports to
cells: Senior management or a board-level committee

rows.label: Independence
cells: Part of management; some separation from operations

rows.label: Typical limit
cells: May overlook or rationalize weak controls
May be impaired by reporting through management
Periodic, risk-based coverage; less operational exposure

subtopics.example: The compliance team of a Hong Kong brokerage reports that all trading controls passed its monitoring, and the audit committee asks whether an internal audit is still needed. Ka-yan, an internal auditor, explains that compliance is a second-line role inside management, so its monitoring is not independent assurance. Ka-yan proposes that internal audit review the monitoring's quality and rely on it where it holds up.

review: Evaluate the competence, objectivity and methods of second-line monitoring before relying on it
Compare second-line results with the internal auditors' own sample tests
evidence: Reperformed sample of the second line's monitoring tests
Written rationale for using, or not using, another team's test results
audit_focus.recommend: Have the chief audit executive show the board where second-line work was used and where coverage gaps remain.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive chooses whether to rely; the board keeps sight of it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Independence is highest in the third line. Second-line monitoring is management's own work, so internal audit gives assurance over it. Must: to rely on another provider's work, the chief audit executive documents the basis and stays responsible for the conclusions.

exam_traps.trap: If risk management and compliance already checked an area, internal audit should leave it alone.
exam_traps.why: Coordination avoids waste, but the third line also gives assurance over the second line. Reliance is a choice made after evaluating that work.

exam_traps.trap: Outsourcing internal audit or a compliance task makes it independent.
exam_traps.why: Hiring an outside firm does not change which line the work belongs to. What counts is which function directs the firm.

key_terms.definition: A table of significant risks and who gives assurance over each.
Using another party's work or information instead of repeating it, after judging it trustworthy.

subtopics.name: First-Line and Second-Line Duties That Impair Independence
subtopics.definition: Impairing duties are first-line or second-line responsibilities, such as deciding risk responses, owning policies or running controls, that the internal audit function cannot hold and still assess objectively.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An internal auditor who decides the response to a risk will later be asked whether that decision was sound. Nobody assesses their own work objectively.
how_it_works: A second 2026 Statement of Position, on enterprise risk management, says internal audit must not determine, prioritize, select, implement or own risk responses.
It must not take over management's follow-up of actions, or own the organization's reporting to external parties.
It should not own final policies, or run a continuing risk assessment process and then audit that same process.
The board sets risk appetite. Internal audit gives assurance on whether it is established and built into decisions (how: see 1C6.1 and 1C6.2).
Internal audit may still advise: suggest methods, facilitate workshops and training, challenge assumptions and share good practice.
For its own planning it still assesses risks, keeps the audit universe and consolidates assurance results.
subtopics.example: At a Peruvian mining company, the chief operating officer asks internal audit to keep the corporate risk register and choose the response to each risk. Milagros, an internal auditor, explains that deciding how to respond to each risk is management's responsibility. Milagros offers to facilitate a risk workshop instead and refers the request to the chief audit executive.

review: Inspect the charter and job descriptions for management duties held by internal auditors
Identify risk response plans or policy documents that an internal auditor signed
evidence: Risk committee minutes naming the person who approved each risk response
Charter section describing internal audit's role in risk management
audit_focus.recommend: Assign a first-line or second-line manager as owner of each risk response, policy and action tracker; senior management names them.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides risk responses and is accountable to the board

subtopics.isaca_rule: Internal audit may advise, facilitate and challenge. Under The IIA's Statement of Position it must not decide, select, implement or own risk responses, and should not own policies. A task that makes internal audit the owner of what it later assesses belongs to management.

exam_traps.trap: Internal audit knows the risks best, so it should choose the risk responses.
exam_traps.why: Choosing and implementing responses is management decision-making. Internal audit gives assurance on whether responses are adequate and may advise on options.

exam_traps.trap: Facilitating a risk workshop is a second-line duty internal audit must refuse.
exam_traps.why: Facilitation, training and challenge are advisory services internal audit may provide, as long as management owns the outputs.

key_terms.definition: What management chooses to do about a risk.
How much risk, and which kinds, an organization is prepared to take for its strategy.
Internal audit's list of the units, processes and systems that could be audited.

subtopics.name: Safeguards When Internal Audit Takes On Other Roles
subtopics.definition: Safeguards are the measures that keep assurance credible when the internal audit function, or the chief audit executive (CAE), does first-line or second-line work or appears to.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Small organizations and urgent situations can leave nobody else to do the job. That is allowed only with transparency, board approval and independent assurance.
how_it_works: The CAE must discuss the role with the board and senior management and advise on safeguards for actual, potential or perceived impairments (Standard 7.1 Organizational Independence).
For an ongoing role, the charter must document the responsibilities, nature of work and safeguards. The board approves the wider remit.
If that area is audited, another route to assurance must be set up, such as an outside provider reporting to the board.
For a temporary role, outside assurance must continue for 12 months after it ends, and a plan returns the work to management.
Assurance engagements over a function the CAE runs must have oversight from an independent party outside internal audit.
subtopics.example: An Icelandic pension fund has no compliance officer, so the board asks Sigrun, the CAE, to run compliance monitoring permanently. Sigrun explains the self-review bias and proposes safeguards, which the board approves: the charter describes the duties, and an outside firm audits compliance and reports to the board. Sigrun confirms the safeguards in the next independence report.

review: Compare duties held outside auditing with what the charter says about them
Confirm someone independent reviewed every area that internal audit itself runs
evidence: External reviewer's report on those areas, addressed to the board
Board resolution accepting the added duties, with the risks they bring
Dated handover schedule for any duty held only for a time
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the board to commission an external review of any area where internal audit performs management duties.
audit_focus.decides: The board accepts the added duty and acknowledges the impairment

subtopics.isaca_rule: A safeguard never lets internal audit audit itself. Must: for a role beyond internal auditing, the CAE discusses it with the board and senior management, documents an ongoing role in the charter, and arranges outside assurance, for 12 more months after a temporary role.

exam_traps.trap: With good safeguards, internal audit can give assurance over the compliance work it performs.
exam_traps.why: The safeguard is that an independent party assures that area or oversees the engagement. Internal audit cannot assure its own second-line work.

exam_traps.trap: Once a temporary role is handed back, internal audit can audit that area at once.
exam_traps.why: Outside assurance runs for 12 months after the role ends. That forward 12 months is separate from the look-back 12 months on an internal auditor's former responsibility.

key_terms.definition: A competent, objective provider outside both internal audit and the area concerned that gives assurance and reports to the board.
Something that looks like an impairment of independence or objectivity even when none exists.

key_terminologies.Purpose of Internal Auditing: Domain I of the Standards: why internal auditing exists and the conditions under which it works best.
key_terminologies.Global Internal Audit Standards: The IIA's standards for the profession, published in 2024: five domains, 15 principles and 52 standards.
key_terminologies.Consideration for Implementation: A 'should' or 'may' in a standard: preferred or optional practice, not mandatory.
key_terminologies.Internal audit function: The person or team that provides internal audit services; 'the function' for short.
key_terminologies.Chief audit executive (CAE): The head of the internal audit function, whatever the job title.
key_terminologies.Engagement supervisor: The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
key_terminologies.Board: The highest governing body, such as the directors or audit committee; where several govern, the body (or bodies) empowered to give internal audit its mandate.
key_terminologies.Senior management: The top executives, usually including the chief executive officer, who answer to the board.
key_terminologies.Internal audit mandate: What the function may do, the part it plays and what it must deliver; set by the board, by law, or both.
key_terminologies.Internal audit charter: The board-approved document holding the function's mandate, position and reporting lines.
key_terminologies.Essential conditions: Board and senior management activities, not requirements on them, that Domain III lists as necessary for an effective internal audit function.
key_terminologies.Assurance services: Engagements where internal auditors test an activity against criteria and state a conclusion others can rely on.
key_terminologies.Advisory services: Advice, started by internal auditors or on request, with no assurance given and no management responsibility taken on.
key_terminologies.Limited and reasonable assurance: Two levels of audit assurance named in the Standards, which define neither. The level depends on the kind, timing and amount of work done.
key_terminologies.Criteria: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
key_terminologies.Independence: The function's freedom, gained from its position, to do and report its work without being steered by those it audits.
key_terminologies.Objectivity: Each internal auditor's unbiased state of mind when judging evidence.
key_terminologies.Functional reporting: The chief audit executive's direct reporting line to the board.
key_terminologies.Administrative reporting: The chief audit executive's day-to-day line to a member of management, ideally the chief executive officer.
key_terminologies.Impairment: A condition that weakens independence or objectivity, in fact or in appearance.
key_terminologies.Safeguard: A measure that manages an actual, potential or perceived impairment to independence or objectivity, such as reassignment, outside oversight or outside assurance.
key_terminologies.Three Lines Model: The IIA's model of who owns risk, who supports and challenges, and who gives independent assurance.
key_terminologies.First line: Operational management, which owns and manages risk and runs the controls.
key_terminologies.Second line: Management's specialist roles, such as risk management and compliance, that support, monitor and challenge the first line.
key_terminologies.Third line: The internal audit function, which gives independent assurance and advice and reports functionally to the board.
key_terminologies.Topical Requirement: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
key_terminologies.Right-to-audit clause: A contract term that lets the organization or its auditors examine a third party's records and controls.
key_terminologies.Control self-assessment: A process in which managers and staff evaluate the risks and controls in their own area.
